concepts.title: Containers vs Virtual Machines: Namespaces and Cgroups
concepts.description: A container is not a lightweight virtual machine. It is a set of ordinary Linux processes that the kernel has been told to isolate using namespaces and to meter using cgroups, running on the same kernel the host is already running.
learningObjectives: Explain what a Linux namespace is and name at least four kinds Docker relies on (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user).
Explain what a cgroup is, and how limiting resource usage differs from isolating a view of a resource.
Explain why a container shares the host's kernel while a VM does not, and what that implies for startup time.
Predict the difference between a process's PID inside a container and its PID as seen from the host.
Explain why a kernel vulnerability is a bigger risk for container isolation than for VM isolation.

sections.heading: Two Different Games: Hardware Virtualization vs OS-Level Virtualization
sections.body:
A virtual machine works by virtualizing hardware. A hypervisor (using CPU features like Intel VT-x or AMD-V) emulates a complete virtual computer (virtual CPU, memory, disk, and network card), and a full, independent operating system, kernel included, boots inside that emulated hardware. Two VMs on the same physical host are running two separate kernels; neither has any built-in awareness that it's sharing hardware with the other.

A container works differently and doesn't involve a hypervisor. There is one kernel running, the host's, and every container on that host is a set of ordinary processes managed by that one kernel, just like any other process you might start directly. A container image never contains a kernel; it contains userspace files only (a C library, some coreutils, maybe a package manager, your application and its dependencies). The 'operating system' a container image claims to be based on (Ubuntu, Alpine, Debian) refers only to that userspace layer. Swap the host's kernel for a different one and every container on it uses that kernel, because there's no separate kernel bundled inside any of them.

sections.heading: Namespaces: The Illusion of Being Alone
sections.body:
A **namespace** is a kernel feature that gives a group of processes their own private view of some global resource, rather than the one shared view every process would otherwise see. Docker relies on several kinds: a **pid** namespace gives a container its own process tree, numbered from 1, with no visibility into processes outside it; a **net** namespace gives it its own network interfaces, IP addresses, routing table, and port space; a **mnt** namespace gives it its own filesystem mount table, which is what makes the layered image filesystem (covered in the next concept) possible in the first place; a **uts** namespace gives it its own hostname; an **ipc** namespace isolates shared memory and semaphores; and a **user** namespace can map a user that looks like root inside the container to an unprivileged, ordinary user outside it, limiting what a compromised 'root' process inside a container can actually do to the host.

Docker did not invent any of this; namespaces existed in the Linux kernel for years before Docker packaged them into a convenient tool. What Docker adds is the tooling: automatically creating the right set of namespaces, wiring them together sensibly, and pairing them with an image format, so you get 'container isolation' with one command instead of manually assembling several kernel primitives by hand.

sections.heading: Cgroups: Rationing, Not Isolation
sections.body:
Namespaces answer the question 'what can this process see?' **Cgroups** (control groups) answer a completely different question: 'how much of a shared resource can this process use, and what happens if it tries to use more?' A cgroup organizes a set of processes into an accounting and limiting group for CPU time, memory, block IO, and more -- it doesn't hide anything from anyone; it enforces a ceiling.

`docker run --memory=256m` sets a cgroup memory limit of 256MB on the container. If the process inside tries to exceed that limit, the kernel's OOM (out-of-memory) killer, operating at the cgroup boundary, terminates a process inside that cgroup. The containment is scoped: it kills something inside this one container's cgroup, not an arbitrary process elsewhere on the host, and it needs no namespace to do so. Cgroups and namespaces are independent mechanisms that happen to be used together. Without a memory limit, a runaway process inside a container can consume host memory without any ceiling, potentially destabilizing every other container (and the host) running alongside it, which is the scenario cgroups are meant to prevent.

sections.heading: Why This Trade-off Gives Fast Starts but a Thinner Isolation Boundary
sections.body:
These two mechanisms explain the practical differences you see. Starting a container means: the kernel creates a handful of namespaces, sets up a cgroup, and starts one process -- work measured in milliseconds. Starting a VM means: the hypervisor allocates memory, emulates a full set of virtual hardware, and boots an entire second kernel from scratch -- work measured in seconds, with a fixed baseline memory and CPU overhead paid whether or not the VM is doing anything useful yet.

The flip side is the isolation boundary itself. Because every container on a host shares the same kernel, a bug that lets a process escape its namespace boundary (a kernel vulnerability, a dangerous Linux capability left enabled, a misconfigured mount) can potentially affect every other container on that host, and the host itself. There is no second kernel acting as a hard backstop the way there is between two VMs on the same hypervisor, where compromising one guest kernel doesn't hand you anything inside the other guest's kernel. This is why security-sensitive, multi-tenant platforms sometimes wrap containers in an additional VM-level boundary (technologies like gVisor, Kata Containers, or Firecracker): namespaces and cgroups are useful isolation, just not as strong a guarantee as a separate kernel.

examples.title: Same Process, Two Different PIDs
examples.code:
# On the host
$ docker run -d --name web nginx:alpine
$ ps aux | grep nginx
root      48213  0.0  0.1  10616  5632 ?        Ss   10:02   0:00 nginx: master process nginx -g daemon off;

# Inside the container's OWN pid namespace
$ docker exec web ps aux
PID   USER     TIME  COMMAND
    1 root      0:00 nginx: master process nginx -g daemon off;
    7 root      0:00 nginx: worker process
examples.explanation: This is one process viewed through two pid namespaces. On the host, it's one more entry in a long, machine-wide process table, labeled with whatever PID was free (48213 here; the exact numbers vary). Inside the container's own pid namespace, it's the first process that namespace started, so it's PID 1, which is special (init-like) just as on a standalone Linux system. Neither number is more correct; they're independent labels from two vantage points onto one process. It's also why, if a container's PID 1 process exits, the whole container stops: the namespace's root process is gone.

examples.title: A cgroup Memory Limit Killing a Container (Exit Code 137)
examples.code:
$ docker run --memory=50m --memory-swap=50m --name hog alpine sh -c "apk add --no-cache stress-ng >/dev/null 2>&1 && stress-ng --vm 1 --vm-bytes 100M --timeout 5s"
$ docker inspect hog --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.ExitCode}}'
true 137
examples.explanation: stress-ng tries to allocate 100MB inside a container whose cgroup memory limit is only 50MB (`--memory-swap=50m` keeps the container from swapping its way past the limit). The kernel's cgroup-aware OOM killer terminates the offending process with SIGKILL; exit code 137 is 128 + 9, the convention for 'killed by signal 9.' `OOMKilled: true` in `docker inspect` confirms this was a memory-limit kill, not an ordinary crash. The exact exit code can differ here, because stress-ng runs its allocator in a child process and the code reported depends on whether the container's main process itself was the one killed. No other container or the host is affected: the limit and the kill are scoped to this container's cgroup, which is the point of setting one.

examples.title: Building a Namespace by Hand With unshare (No Docker Involved)
examples.code:
$ sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc /bin/sh
# ps -eo pid,user,args
    PID USER     COMMAND
      1 root     /bin/sh
      5 root     ps -eo pid,user,args
examples.explanation: `unshare` is a plain Linux utility, unrelated to Docker, that uses the same kernel namespace feature Docker relies on. `--pid --fork` creates a new pid namespace and forks a child process into it; `--mount-proc` mounts a fresh /proc so that `ps` reflects this namespace's view rather than the host's. The shell becomes PID 1 in its own small world, with no visibility into host processes. This is the same primitive `docker run` uses, minus the layered image filesystem and the tooling that makes it feel like one command.

misconceptions.description: A container is essentially a lightweight VM -- it boots its own tiny operating system and kernel inside the container.
misconceptions.clarification: There is no kernel inside a container image. An image only contains userspace files -- a C library, coreutils, a package manager, your application and its dependencies -- layered on top of whatever kernel the host is already running. There's also typically no boot process: the container's PID 1 is usually your application directly, not an init system bringing up virtual hardware. When people say a container is 'based on Ubuntu,' they mean its userspace files came from Ubuntu's package ecosystem -- the kernel underneath is the host's, whatever that happens to be.

misconceptions.description: Namespaces and cgroups together make containers just as strongly isolated from each other, security-wise, as separate VMs would be.
misconceptions.clarification: Every container on a host shares one single kernel, which means one single attack surface -- a kernel vulnerability, a dangerous capability left enabled, or a misconfigured mount can potentially let a process cross its namespace boundary and affect other containers or the host. VMs have independent kernels enforced by a hardware-assisted hypervisor boundary, which is a stronger isolation guarantee than a shared-kernel mechanism can offer. Namespaces and cgroups are useful isolation, just a weaker guarantee than a second kernel, which is why sensitive multi-tenant workloads sometimes wrap containers in an additional VM-level boundary (gVisor, Kata Containers, Firecracker) rather than relying on namespaces and cgroups alone.

exercises.prompt: You start a container with `docker run -d --name app alpine sleep 1000`, then run `docker exec app ps aux` and, separately, `ps aux | grep sleep` on the host itself. What PID does `sleep` show inside the container's own ps output, and is that the same number the host sees for that process?
exercises.code:
$ docker run -d --name app alpine sleep 1000
$ docker exec app ps aux
$ ps aux | grep sleep
hints: Think about what pid namespace remapping means for the very first process started inside a fresh container.

The host's process table and the container's process table are two different views over the same underlying kernel scheduler entries -- the same real process can carry two different PID labels depending on which namespace you're looking from.
PID 1 is special inside a pid namespace -- it's reserved for whichever process that namespace considers its first/root process.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Inside the container, sleep shows up as PID 1, since it's the first (and only) process started in that pid namespace. On the host, the exact same physical process has a different, much larger PID, since it's just one more entry in the host's own, much longer-running process table. Both PIDs refer to the same running process -- there is no 'more real' one, just two different numbering views.
exercises.solutionExplanation: docker exec app ps aux runs ps inside app's own pid namespace, where sleep was the very first process ever started in that namespace, so it's labeled PID 1 there -- pid namespaces number processes from 1 within their own namespace, independent of any numbering happening anywhere else. ps aux | grep sleep on the host runs in the host's own pid namespace, which sees every process on the machine, including this one, labeled with whatever host-wide PID was next available, e.g. 48213. Both commands are looking at the same process; they're two independent labelings from two namespace vantage points.

exercises.prompt: A monitoring sidecar is supposed to watch only its own container's process and restart it if it uses too much CPU. Someone launched it with --pid=host 'to make it easier to see the process,' and now the sidecar's cleanup logic occasionally kills an unrelated process on the HOST, not the one it was supposed to manage. Find the bug and fix it.
hints: --pid=host doesn't just make the host's processes visible -- think about what pid namespace the sidecar's own process-table lookups now operate in.
Without --pid=host, what pid namespace would the sidecar be watching, and could 48213 even mean anything at all in that namespace?
The real fix isn't a smarter PID number -- it's giving the sidecar its own isolated pid namespace and identifying its target some other way.
exercises.solutionCode:
# Don't share the host's pid namespace at all -- let the sidecar keep its own,
# and identify the target container by name/label through the Docker API instead of a raw host PID.
$ docker run -d --name sidecar mymonitor:latest --target-container=app
exercises.solutionExplanation: --pid=host drops the sidecar into the HOST's pid namespace instead of giving it its own, so every PID the sidecar sees or acts on, including '48213', is a host-wide PID, not a number scoped to one container. Host PIDs get recycled on a busy machine, so if the process behind 48213 has exited and the host has reassigned that number to something unrelated, the sidecar's 'restart if using too much CPU' logic can end up signaling that unrelated process. The fix is not to share the host pid namespace at all: let the sidecar keep its own pid namespace and identify its target through something namespace-independent, like the Docker API or a container name, rather than a raw numeric PID that only means something relative to one pid namespace.

assessments.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a container from a virtual machine?
options: The only real difference is that VMs are for Windows workloads and containers are for Linux workloads.
A VM and a container both share the host's kernel, but a VM additionally encrypts its filesystem.

A container is a set of processes isolated by kernel namespaces and metered by cgroups, all running on the one kernel the host is already running; a VM runs a separate kernel under hardware-assisted virtualization.
A container includes its own kernel, just a smaller one than a full VM's kernel.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer is the technical distinction: containers achieve isolation and resource limits entirely within a single shared kernel via namespaces and cgroups, while VMs virtualize hardware itself so each guest boots and runs its own independent kernel. The “A container includes its own kernel, just…” option is wrong -- container images ship userspace files only, never a kernel. The “A VM and a container both share…” option is wrong on its first clause (VMs do NOT share the host kernel; containers do) and invents an unrelated encryption claim. The “The only real difference is that VMs…” option is wrong: the kernel-sharing distinction is the difference, and it has nothing to do with which guest OS family is running (Linux containers needing a Linux host kernel is a consequence of the mechanism).

assessments.prompt: A process inside a container binds to port 5432. A completely unrelated process on the host is already using port 5432 for something else. Which namespace explains why this doesn't cause a conflict?
options: The net namespace, which gives the container its own network interfaces, IP addresses, and port space.
The pid namespace, since it isolates process IDs, not ports.
The mnt namespace, since ports are represented as files under /proc.
The uts namespace, which isolates hostname and therefore also isolates ports bound under that hostname.
assessments.explanation: The net namespace gives a container its own network interfaces, IP addresses, routing table, and port space, so a process inside it binding to port 5432 has no automatic relationship to port 5432 on the host or in any other namespace -- they're simply independent port spaces. The “The pid namespace, since it isolates process…” option is wrong -- the pid namespace isolates process ID numbering, not networking. The “The mnt namespace, since ports are represented…” option is wrong -- the mnt namespace isolates the filesystem mount table, which is unrelated to port binding even though /proc happens to expose some network state as files. The “The uts namespace, which isolates hostname…” option is wrong -- the uts namespace only isolates the hostname string, with no relationship to port allocation at all.

assessments.prompt: A container is started with `docker run --memory=100m`, and the process inside attempts to allocate 500MB. What actually happens, and what is the scope of the resulting action?
options: The entire host immediately reboots to reclaim memory.
Docker silently raises the memory limit to whatever the process actually requested.
The allocation attempt is queued and retried indefinitely until memory becomes available.
The kernel's cgroup-aware OOM killer terminates a process inside that specific container's cgroup with SIGKILL; other containers and the host itself are unaffected.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer: exceeding the limit triggers the kernel's OOM killer, but scoped specifically to that container's own cgroup, terminating a process within it (commonly surfacing as exit code 137, 128+9 for SIGKILL) without touching any other container or the host. The “The entire host immediately reboots to reclaim memory” option overstates the blast radius; cgroups exist to contain this kind of failure to one container. The “Docker silently raises the memory limit…” option is wrong -- Docker enforces the limit rather than adjusting it on demand. The “The allocation attempt is queued and retried…” option is wrong -- there's no retry-and-wait behavior; the kernel acts immediately once the limit is exceeded.

assessments.prompt: Why might a security-sensitive, multi-tenant platform run containers inside an additional VM-level boundary (gVisor, Kata Containers, or Firecracker) instead of relying on namespaces and cgroups alone?
options: Because namespaces are deprecated in modern Linux kernels and require a compatibility shim to keep working.
Because every container on a shared-kernel host is still exposed to the same kernel.
Because cgroups cannot enforce memory limits on multi-tenant hosts, only on single-tenant ones.
Because namespaces and cgroups only function correctly on a single-tenant host.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer: namespaces and cgroups are real isolation, but they all sit on top of one shared kernel, so any gap in that shared attack surface can potentially cross container boundaries, a risk a separate guest kernel doesn't share. The “Because namespaces and cgroups only function correctly…” option is false -- namespaces and cgroups work identically regardless of tenancy model; the concern is about isolation strength, not functionality. The “Because cgroups cannot enforce memory limits…” option is false -- cgroup memory enforcement has nothing to do with how many tenants a host serves. The “Because namespaces are deprecated in modern Linux…” option is false and invents a deprecation that hasn't happened -- namespaces remain the core mechanism containers rely on today.

assessments.prompt: A colleague asks: 'If containers don't have their own kernel, why do they start so much faster than VMs, and what do we actually give up by taking that shortcut?' Give a full answer.
assessments.modelAnswer: Containers start fast because starting one is cheap at the kernel level: the host kernel creates a handful of namespaces (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, and optionally user), sets up a cgroup to meter resource usage, and starts one process inside that isolated view, all of which takes milliseconds, since no hardware is being emulated and no second kernel needs to boot. A VM, by contrast, requires a hypervisor to allocate memory, emulate an entire set of virtual hardware, and boot a completely independent guest kernel from scratch, which takes seconds and carries a fixed memory and CPU overhead whether or not the VM is doing anything useful yet. What we give up for that speed is the strength of the isolation boundary. Every container on a host shares the same kernel, so a kernel vulnerability, a dangerous Linux capability left enabled, or a misconfigured mount can potentially let a process escape its namespace boundary and affect other containers or the host. There's no second kernel acting as a hard backstop the way there is between two VMs on the same hypervisor, where compromising one guest's kernel doesn't hand you anything inside a sibling guest's kernel. That's why sensitive multi-tenant workloads sometimes accept the slower startup and wrap containers in an additional VM-level boundary, using technologies like gVisor, Kata Containers, or Firecracker, treating namespaces and cgroups as useful isolation, just not as strong a guarantee as a separate kernel.

concepts.title: Images, Containers, and the Layered (Union) Filesystem
concepts.description: An image is a stack of read-only layers built from a Dockerfile; a container is a running instance of that stack with one thin writable layer added on top -- understanding this union filesystem explains why containers start in milliseconds, why running many of them barely multiplies disk usage, and why layer order in a Dockerfile matters.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between an image and a container in terms of filesystem layers.
Explain what a union filesystem is and why Docker uses one (OverlayFS) to assemble a container's filesystem.
Explain why multiple containers can share the same image's layers without duplicating disk space.
Explain what happens at the filesystem level when a running container modifies a file that exists in a lower read-only layer (copy-on-write).
Predict how removing a container affects the image it came from, and vice versa.

sections.heading: An Image Is a Stack of Read-Only Layers
sections.body:
When Docker builds an image from a Dockerfile, it doesn't produce one big blob of files. Each instruction that changes the filesystem (mainly RUN, COPY, and ADD) produces its own layer: a self-contained diff of what changed relative to the layer below it. The final image is an ordered list of these layers plus a small amount of metadata: the image manifest lists which layers in which order, and the image config holds the default command, exposed ports, environment variables, and so on.

Each layer is identified by a content hash of its own contents, not by a name you chose or a position in a list. This has a useful consequence: if two unrelated images both start FROM python:3.11-slim, Docker recognizes their first several layers as byte-for-byte identical (same hash) and stores that data once on disk, no matter how many images or containers reference it. You pay disk cost per unique layer, not per image, so a Docker host running dozens of images built from a handful of common bases shares a lot of its data.

Layers are read-only once built. An image is immutable: you cannot reach into layer 3 of a built image and edit a file in place. The only way to change what an image contains is to add a new layer on top, ideally by rebuilding from a Dockerfile, a discipline the last section of this concept returns to.

sections.heading: A Container Adds Exactly One Writable Layer on Top
sections.body:
docker run does not copy an image's files anywhere. It takes the image's stack of read-only layers as they already sit on disk and mounts a new, empty writable layer on top of them using a union filesystem. OverlayFS (the overlay2 storage driver) is the standard on modern Linux; older setups used AUFS or devicemapper. From inside the container, the filesystem looks like a single, ordinary, unified tree; in reality it's several layers merged on the fly by the kernel, with the writable layer taking priority at the top.

Reads are resolved top-down: to open a file, the kernel checks the writable layer first, and if it's not there, falls through to the next layer down, and the next, until it finds the file (or fails, if no layer has it). Writes are more interesting. If a container modifies a file that only exists in a lower, read-only layer, the union filesystem can't edit that lower layer in place -- it's read-only, and might be shared with other containers and images besides. So it performs a copy-up: the file is copied, in full, from the lower layer into the container's own writable layer first, and only then is the modification applied to that new copy. From then on, this container sees its own modified copy in the writable layer; every other container built from the same image still sees the original in the shared lower layer. Deleting a file that exists in a lower layer works similarly, via a whiteout marker written into the writable layer that tells the union filesystem to hide that path. The bytes are still in the lower layer, hidden but not erased.

sections.heading: Why This Makes Containers Cheap to Start and Cheap to Multiply
sections.body:
This layering model is why containers start in milliseconds and cost so little to run side by side. Starting a container never copies an image's contents; it's a union mount of layers already on disk plus one small, empty writable layer, followed by starting a single process inside the namespaces from the previous concept. None of that scales with image size the way you might expect; a 2GB image and a 20MB image mount in roughly the same amount of time, because mounting existing layers is cheap regardless of how much data they contain.

It also explains why ten containers from the same image use nowhere near ten times the disk of one. All ten share the same read-only layers, which exist once on disk, and each adds only its own writable layer, which stays small unless the workload writes a lot (logs, temp files, an in-container database with no volume). Ten VMs would each need their own mostly duplicated disk image and OS boot's worth of memory overhead.

sections.heading: Images Are Immutable: docker commit Is a Trap
sections.body:
Because the writable layer is just another layer, Docker lets you turn it into a new image with docker commit <container> new-image-name, freezing whatever the container's writable layer currently contains. It works as a shortcut: exec into a running container, install a missing package or tweak a config file until things work, then docker commit to 'save' that state as a new image.

Don't. The resulting image's contents exist only in that one binary blob, with no readable, diffable, version-controllable record of what changed or why, the way a Dockerfile instruction is. Six months later nobody (including you) can reconstruct how it came to be, and rebuilding after a base image security patch means redoing the manual work from memory, because there's no script to rerun. Representing an image as Dockerfile instructions makes the recipe the source of truth: checked into version control next to your application code and rebuildable by anyone (assuming pinned versions, covered in the next concept) without remembering what was typed inside a live container. Treat a running container's writable layer as scratch space, not as where your image's definition lives.

examples.title: One Image, Two Containers, Shared Disk
examples.code:
$ docker pull ubuntu:22.04
$ docker run -d --name svc_a ubuntu:22.04 sleep 3600
$ docker run -d --name svc_b ubuntu:22.04 sleep 3600
$ docker ps -s --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Image}}\t{{.Size}}"
NAMES   IMAGE          SIZE
svc_b   ubuntu:22.04   0B (virtual 77.9MB)
svc_a   ubuntu:22.04   0B (virtual 77.9MB)
examples.explanation: svc_a and svc_b both start from the same ubuntu:22.04 image, and each gets its own writable layer, but neither has written anything meaningful yet, so each is reported at 0B. The image's 77.9MB exists once on disk; the 'virtual' 77.9MB is everything each container can see (its own writable layer plus the shared read-only layers beneath it), not 77.9MB duplicated per container. Start a hundred more containers from that image and its on-disk footprint doesn't grow; only the (typically tiny) writable layers of the new containers do.

examples.title: Copy-on-Write, Made Visible With docker diff
examples.code:
$ docker run -dit --name box ubuntu:22.04 bash
$ docker exec box bash -c "echo '# local tweak' >> /etc/profile"
$ docker exec box bash -c "rm /etc/issue"
$ docker exec box bash -c "echo hi > /tmp/scratch.txt"
$ docker diff box
C /etc
D /etc/issue
C /etc/profile
C /tmp
A /tmp/scratch.txt
examples.explanation: docker diff reads the container's writable layer and reports three kinds of change relative to the image: C (changed: /etc/profile was copied up from the image's lower layer into the writable layer, then appended to; parent directories such as /etc show as changed too), A (added: /tmp/scratch.txt never existed in the image and lives only in this container's writable layer), and D (deleted: /etc/issue still exists in the image's lower layer, but a whiteout marker in the writable layer hides it from this container). None of this touched the underlying ubuntu:22.04 image: a new container from that image would have the original /etc/issue and /etc/profile and no /tmp/scratch.txt. (The files Docker manages itself, /etc/hostname, /etc/hosts, and /etc/resolv.conf, are bind-mounted into the container and don't show up in docker diff.)

examples.title: Why Editing a Running Container Doesn't Update Anyone Else's Image
examples.code:
$ docker run -dit --name teammate_a myapp:1.0 bash
$ docker exec teammate_a bash -c "echo 'FEATURE_FLAG=true' >> /app/.env"
# Meanwhile, a teammate starts a fresh container from the SAME image tag:
$ docker run -dit --name teammate_b myapp:1.0 bash
$ docker exec teammate_b cat /app/.env
# FEATURE_FLAG=true is NOT there -- teammate_b's .env matches the original image's
examples.explanation: teammate_a's edit landed in teammate_a's own writable layer and nowhere else; the myapp:1.0 image is unchanged. teammate_b's container has a separate writable layer on top of the same unmodified image layers, so it never sees the change. The only way to make that FEATURE_FLAG line show up for every future container is to put it in the Dockerfile (or a file that gets COPYed in) and rebuild, producing a new tag that every teammate pulls. Editing a running container is a per-container, throwaway action, not a way to update the shared, named artifact everyone else pulls.

misconceptions.description: docker run copies all of an image's files into a fresh directory for the new container, so starting a container from a much larger image takes proportionally longer.
misconceptions.clarification: No copying happens. docker run mounts the image's existing read-only layers (already sitting on disk from the pull/build) using a union filesystem, and adds one small, initially-empty writable layer on top. Because nothing gets duplicated, the time to start a container is essentially independent of image size -- a 2GB image and a 20MB image mount in roughly the same time. What actually varies startup time is the application itself (interpreter start, framework initialization, dependency loading at runtime), not Docker's own layer-mounting step.

misconceptions.description: Manually fixing something inside a running container and running docker commit is basically equivalent to editing the Dockerfile and rebuilding -- both end up as 'an image with the fix in it.'
misconceptions.clarification: They produce superficially similar images but are not equivalent processes. A Dockerfile rebuild leaves a readable, versionable record of exactly what changed and why, reproducible by anyone with the same Dockerfile and base image; a docker commit freezes whatever a container's writable layer happens to contain into an opaque blob with no record of which specific actions produced it. The commit approach also diverges from your actual Dockerfile: the next rebuild from it won't include whatever you patched by hand, so the fix disappears the next time someone does a normal build, and whoever hits the bug again months later has no idea it was ever 'already fixed.'

exercises.prompt: A container named box is started from an image whose /etc/motd file (a lower, read-only layer) contains the text 'Welcome'. Inside the running container, someone overwrites that file. What does a brand-new container started fresh from the same image print when it reads /etc/motd, and why?
exercises.code:
$ docker exec box bash -c "echo 'Hi there' > /etc/motd"
$ docker exec box cat /etc/motd
$ docker run --rm same_image cat /etc/motd
hints: The write happened inside box's own writable layer -- think about whether that layer is shared with anything else, including a brand-new container from the same image.
Overwriting a file that exists in a lower, read-only layer triggers a copy-up into the writable layer first -- where does that copy end up living, and who else can see it?
A brand-new docker run mounts the image's layers plus its OWN fresh, empty writable layer -- not box's.
exercises.expectedAnswer: docker exec box cat /etc/motd prints 'Hi there' (box's own writable layer now has the modified file). docker run --rm same_image cat /etc/motd prints the original 'Welcome' -- the new container gets a brand-new, empty writable layer stacked on the same unmodified read-only image layers, and never sees anything from box's writable layer.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Overwriting /etc/motd inside box triggers a copy-up: the file is copied from the image's read-only layer into box's own writable layer, and the write happens to that copy -- box's writable layer now holds 'Hi there', while the image's underlying layer still holds the original 'Welcome', completely untouched. A brand-new docker run from the same image never touches box's writable layer at all; it mounts the same shared read-only layers plus a brand-new, independent, empty writable layer of its own. Since that new container's writable layer never received box's copy-up, reading /etc/motd falls through to the shared lower layer and finds the original, unmodified 'Welcome'.

exercises.prompt: A teammate is confused: they ran a container, docker exec'd in, installed a missing curl binary so a health-check script would work, confirmed it worked, and moved on. A week later, a fresh deploy pulls the same image tag and the health check fails again with 'curl: not found.' They insist they already fixed this. What actually happened, and what should they do instead?
exercises.code:
$ docker run -d --name web myapp:2.3
$ docker exec web sh -c "apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl"
$ docker exec web curl -s localhost:8080/health   # works!
# ...one week and one redeploy later...
$ docker run -d --name web2 myapp:2.3
$ docker exec web2 curl -s localhost:8080/health   # curl: not found
hints: Where did apt-get install actually write the curl binary -- into the image myapp:2.3, or into something scoped to just that one running container?
The redeploy started a brand new container from the same image tag. Does a new container inherit anything from a previous container's writable layer?
The durable fix has to change the image itself -- which artifact actually gets rebuilt and repulled on every deploy?
exercises.solutionCode:
# Dockerfile
FROM myapp:2.3
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
# then: docker build -t myapp:2.4 .
# and redeploy using myapp:2.4 (or re-tag/overwrite 2.3 if that's your convention)
exercises.solutionExplanation: The apt-get install run via docker exec modifies only web's own writable layer; it never touches the myapp:2.3 image on disk. The fix the teammate confirmed was real, but it was scoped to that one disposable container. A week later the redeploy starts a new container (web2) from the same unmodified myapp:2.3 image, with its own empty writable layer, so curl is missing again, as if the original fix had never happened, because from the image's perspective it never did. The durable fix has to change the image: add the apt-get install curl step as a Dockerfile instruction, rebuild to produce a new image (or overwrite the same tag, if that's the team's convention), and make sure every future deploy pulls that rebuilt image.

assessments.prompt: A container modifies a file that currently exists only in one of its image's lower, read-only layers. What actually happens at the filesystem level?
options: The modification is written directly to the writable layer with no relation to the original file, effectively creating a brand-new, unrelated file at the same path.
Docker rejects the write, since read-only layers cannot be modified.
The read-only layer is temporarily unlocked, modified in place, and re-locked when the container stops.
The file is copied from the read-only layer into the container's own writable layer first, and the modification is applied to that copy.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer describes copy-on-write: a copy-up moves the file into the writable layer first, and only that copy is modified. The original stays as it was in the shared, read-only layer, which is why other containers sharing that layer never see the change. The “Docker rejects the write, since read-only layers…” option is wrong: the write succeeds from the container's point of view; it just doesn't happen where you might assume. The “The read-only layer is temporarily unlocked, modified…” option is wrong -- read-only layers are never unlocked or edited in place; that would break every other container/image sharing them. The “The modification is written directly…” option is subtly wrong: the copy-up preserves the file's original content as the starting point before the modification is applied -- it's not an unrelated blank file, it genuinely starts as a copy.

assessments.prompt: A running container deletes a file that exists in one of its image's lower, read-only layers. What actually happens at the filesystem level?
options: A lightweight whiteout marker is written into the container's own writable layer that hides the path from view, while the file's bytes remain physically present, untouched, in the lower layer underneath.
Docker rejects the deletion, since files in read-only layers cannot be removed by a running container.
The file is moved into a separate, hidden "deleted files" layer that other containers can still browse.
The file is physically erased from the read-only layer immediately.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer describes the whiteout mechanism: a delete inside a container never touches the shared, read-only layer beneath it. It writes a marker into the container's own writable layer telling the union filesystem to hide that path for this container, while the original bytes stay in the lower layer, still visible to any other container or image sharing it. The “The file is physically erased…” option is wrong -- nothing in a lower, shared, read-only layer is ever physically erased by a container-level delete. The “Docker rejects the deletion, since files…” option is wrong -- the delete visibly succeeds from the container's own point of view; it just doesn't work the way a delete on an ordinary single-layer filesystem would. The “The file is moved into a separate…” option invents a mechanism ('deleted files layer') that doesn't exist.

assessments.prompt: Why is `docker commit` considered a poor substitute for fixing a Dockerfile and rebuilding, even though both approaches can produce "an image with the fix in it"?
options: docker commit requires the container to be stopped first, while a Dockerfile rebuild can be done on a live container.
docker commit always produces a strictly larger image than an equivalent Dockerfile rebuild.

docker commit freezes whatever the container's writable layer currently contains into an opaque blob with no readable, diffable record of what changed or why, and it silently diverges from the actual Dockerfile, so the fix quietly disappears the next time someone does a normal rebuild.
docker commit is only available on Docker Desktop, not on Linux hosts running the Docker daemon directly.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer is the reason docker commit is a poor workflow: it captures a point-in-time snapshot with no record of the specific actions that produced it, and because it never touches the Dockerfile, the next legitimate rebuild from that Dockerfile silently omits the fix, often resurfacing the exact same bug for someone with no idea it was 'already fixed' once. The “docker commit always produces a strictly larger…” option makes an unsupported size claim that isn't the actual argument made. The “docker commit requires the container…” option is false -- docker commit works on running or stopped containers, and neither approach has a live-editing requirement in the way described. The “docker commit is only available on Docker…” option is false -- docker commit is a standard Docker CLI command available anywhere the Docker daemon runs.

assessments.prompt: Explain, referencing layers and copy-on-write specifically, why ten containers started from the same 2GB image don't use anywhere near 20GB of disk, and why none of them can accidentally corrupt what the others see.
assessments.modelAnswer: An image's contents live in a fixed set of read-only layers, each identified by a content hash and stored on disk once, no matter how many containers or images reference it. Starting a container never copies that data; it mounts the existing layers via a union filesystem and adds one new, tiny writable layer on top. So ten containers from the same 2GB image share that 2GB on disk; the additional cost of the tenth is only its own writable layer, which starts near zero and grows only with what that container writes (logs, temp files, and so on). That writable-layer isolation is also why the containers can't corrupt each other's view: any write inside one container either creates a new file in its own writable layer, or triggers a copy-up of an existing file into that private layer before modifying it. Either way the change is confined to that container's layer; the shared read-only layers are never touched, so every other container keeps seeing the original data regardless of what a sibling does to its own copy.

concepts.title: Why Containers Shrink 'It Works on My Machine'
concepts.description: Containers don't eliminate environment drift by magic. They remove most dependency and configuration drift by packaging an application together with its exact runtime environment into one portable, versioned artifact, leaving only the host kernel, CPU architecture, and available resources as remaining variables.
learningObjectives: List the categories of hidden environment a running application depends on (runtime version, OS libraries, environment variables, config paths, timezone/locale, installed system packages) and state which of these a container image pins down.
Explain what a container does NOT isolate you from: host kernel version/features, CPU architecture, and available host resources.
Explain why a floating base image tag like latest undermines reproducibility, and what pinning a specific tag or digest buys you instead.
Trace a realistic 'worked in dev, broke in CI/prod' bug to a specific unpinned dependency, and explain how containerizing it would (or wouldn't) have caught the bug earlier.
Explain why 'it works in a container on my machine' is a meaningfully stronger claim than 'it works on my machine' alone, without overstating how strong that claim is.

sections.heading: What 'Works on My Machine' Actually Depends On
sections.body: 'Works on my machine' bugs rarely come from the application's own logic, because the source code is identical. They come from everything around the code differing between two machines: the exact version of the language runtime installed (a Python 3.9 versus 3.11 upgrade changes real, documented default behaviors); the versions of shared system libraries the runtime or its native extensions link against (a different OpenSSL build can change which TLS versions or cipher suites are even available); which system packages happen to already be installed globally; environment variables set, or not set, in a developer's shell profile from some long-forgotten setup step; file paths that exist on one machine and not another; and locale and timezone settings, which can change how dates parse, how strings sort, or how numbers format. None of this shows up in a diff of the code. It's the invisible half of the environment the code runs in, and a plain clone-the-repo-and-run-it workflow does nothing to standardize it.

sections.heading: What an Image Pins Down
sections.body: A Dockerfile is an ordered recipe, starting from a base image, for constructing one filesystem: which OS package manager runs which install commands, which language runtime and version gets installed, which application dependencies get resolved and at which versions, which environment variables get set, which files get copied in and where. Build that recipe into an image and (assuming every step is itself pinned to specific versions, a discipline you still have to bring, covered below) you get one fixed artifact. A rebuild yields the same contents, though not necessarily the same bytes or digest. Pull that exact image, by tag or, more strongly, by digest, on your laptop, in CI, or on a production host, and you get the identical userspace: same runtime version, same library versions, same installed packages, same environment variables, same file layout. The whole category of 'old OpenSSL on your laptop, newer one on the server' bugs can't occur, because only one OpenSSL is involved: the one installed inside the image, whatever the host has.

sections.heading: What Containers Still Don't Solve
sections.body: Containers share the host's kernel, and that's where the guarantee runs out. The kernel version and the features and syscalls it supports still vary host to host, and an image built assuming a newer kernel feature can fail on an older host kernel even though every file inside the image is identical. CPU architecture is a second, very common gap: an image built on an Apple Silicon (arm64) laptop and one built on a typical x86-64 (amd64) server are not interchangeable -- a binary compiled for one architecture cannot execute on the other, producing an exec format error that has nothing to do with your Dockerfile being wrong. Available resources are a third: a container that works on a laptop with 32GB of free RAM can behave differently, or get OOM-killed per the cgroups mechanism from the first concept in this module, on a resource-constrained CI runner or a smaller production instance, even from the identical image. No container image can pin these down, because they belong to the host.

sections.heading: Reproducibility Still Requires Discipline: Pinning Tags, Digests, and Dependencies
sections.body: Docker does not force reproducibility on you; it makes it achievable if your Dockerfile avoids floating references. FROM node:latest and FROM node:20 both point at moving targets: a rebuild next month can pull a newer image than a rebuild today, with a different Node.js patch version or different OS package versions in the base. FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim pins a specific version (though a publisher can still re-push a rebuilt image under that tag); FROM node@sha256:<digest> pins a content-addressed image, guaranteeing the exact bytes rather than a tag someone promises not to move. The same discipline has to extend into the Dockerfile's own install steps: apt-get install -y somepackage with no version pin, or pip install requests with no lockfile or version pin, can each resolve to a different package version on two different days, even inside an otherwise reproducible-looking Dockerfile. Containers shrink the surface area where 'works on my machine' bugs can hide, but they make full reproducibility possible, not automatic; you have to write the Dockerfile and its lockfiles as if reproducibility mattered.

examples.title: The Classic Bug: A System Library the Dev Laptop Happened to Have
examples.code:
# Works fine on the developer's laptop:
$ python app.py
Serving on https://localhost:8443  (TLS 1.3 negotiated)

# Fails on a teammate's older Linux box with a system-installed Python 3.9 and an old OpenSSL 1.0.2:
$ python app.py
ssl.SSLError: [SSL: UNSUPPORTED_PROTOCOL] unsupported protocol
examples.explanation: The application code is identical in the failing and working cases; the difference is what's installed underneath it. The developer's laptop has a Python build linked against a modern OpenSSL that supports TLS 1.3; the teammate's older Linux box has an old system Python linked against an OpenSSL that doesn't. Neither setup is wrong, they're different, in a way cloning the repository or reading the code would never reveal. Packaging the app in an image built FROM python:3.11.8-slim-bookworm puts the same OpenSSL in every environment, so the developer, the teammate, and CI all run the same Python build against the same OpenSSL, whatever the host has installed. Containerizing doesn't so much fix the bug as make it impossible to reintroduce, because there's only one OpenSSL in the picture.

examples.title: Floating Tags Changing Underneath You
examples.code:
# Dockerfile written and first built in January -- passes every test.
FROM node:latest
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm install
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

# Rebuilt from the SAME Dockerfile, unmodified, in June:
# $ docker build -t myapp .
#   npm WARN EBADENGINE Unsupported engine ...
#   gyp ERR! build error   (some-native-addon fails to compile against the newer Node)
examples.explanation: Nothing in the Dockerfile changed between January and June, yet the June build fails. node:latest isn't a fixed thing; it's a tag that gets reassigned to the newest published Node image, which by June may be a newer major version than January's. A newer Node can have a different native addon ABI (application binary interface) and different build requirements, so a dependency with a compiled native component that built fine in January's image may fail to compile or load in June's. The fix is to pin an exact version, FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim, so the same Dockerfile produces the same base image whatever date the build runs on.

examples.title: What Still Breaks: CPU Architecture Mismatch
examples.code:
# Built on an Apple Silicon (arm64) laptop:
$ docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
$ docker push myregistry/myapp:1.0

# Deployed to a standard x86-64 (amd64) production EC2 instance:
$ docker run myregistry/myapp:1.0
exec /usr/local/bin/node: exec format error   # older runc: "standard_init_linux.go: exec user process caused: exec format error"
examples.explanation: Every file in the image is identical to what worked on the laptop, and the failure has nothing to do with the Dockerfile or the application's source code. The image's compiled binaries (the runtime itself and any native extensions) were built for the arm64 instruction set, and an amd64 host can't execute arm64 machine code, a hardware-level incompatibility no container abstraction hides. The fix is to build, or have CI build, a multi-architecture image, typically via docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push (multi-platform images are pushed straight to a registry rather than loaded into the local image store), so the registry serves whichever architecture-specific image matches the pulling host automatically.

misconceptions.description: If it runs correctly inside a container on my machine, it's guaranteed to run identically anywhere else, full stop. That's the whole point of containers.
misconceptions.clarification: Containers guarantee a reproducible userspace -- same runtime, same libraries, same packages, same files -- assuming everything was pinned in the Dockerfile. They don't guarantee the same kernel version/features, the same CPU architecture, or the same available resources, because those all belong to whichever host actually runs the container, not to the image. 'Works in a container on my machine' rules out a large category of environment-drift bugs, but it isn't an unconditional guarantee across every host.

misconceptions.description: Docker automatically pins exact versions of everything for me, so as long as I'm using a Dockerfile, my builds are already reproducible.
misconceptions.clarification: Docker gives you the mechanism for reproducibility, a versioned, immutable image format, but nothing forces your Dockerfile to use it responsibly. FROM someimage:latest, an unpinned apt-get install somepackage, or a pip install/npm install with no lockfile can each resolve to different concrete versions on different days, even from an unmodified Dockerfile. You build reproducibility into a Dockerfile through pinned base image tags or digests and pinned dependency versions; you don't get it just because a Dockerfile is involved.

exercises.prompt: Given this Dockerfile, if you run docker build today and again in six months without editing a single line, are the two resulting images guaranteed to be identical? Identify every line that puts that guarantee at risk.
exercises.code:
FROM ubuntu:latest
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3 nginx
COPY . /app
CMD ["python3", "/app/main.py"]
hints: Look specifically at what each line resolves to at build time versus what it literally says in the file -- which lines can resolve to something different on two different days even though the text never changes?
ubuntu:latest is a tag, not a fixed image -- what does that tag point to depend on?
apt-get install -y python3 nginx with no version numbers pulls whatever the currently-configured package repository considers current at build time.
exercises.expectedAnswer: No, not guaranteed. Two lines put reproducibility at risk: FROM ubuntu:latest can resolve to a different, newer Ubuntu base image months later, since the latest tag gets reassigned over time, and apt-get install -y python3 nginx with no version pins can install different concrete package versions depending on whatever the package repository currently serves as 'the' python3/nginx package on the day the build runs. COPY and CMD are deterministic given the same source tree and don't add risk on their own.
exercises.solutionExplanation: FROM ubuntu:latest is a floating reference: the publisher reassigns latest over time to their newest build, so the same Dockerfile line can pull a different base image (different Ubuntu release, different pre-installed package versions) depending on when the build runs. apt-get install -y python3 nginx has the identical problem one layer down: with no version pinned, apt resolves 'python3' and 'nginx' to whatever versions the configured repositories currently serve, which drifts over time as upstream publishes updates. COPY and CMD depend only on your own source tree and the Dockerfile's text, both unchanged here, so they add no risk. Between the two risky lines, a rebuild six months later could pull a newer Ubuntu release with a newer default Python 3.x, install a different nginx, or hit a compatibility issue that didn't exist on day one, though the Dockerfile's text is unchanged.

exercises.prompt: CI has started intermittently failing a build that was passing reliably for months, with no changes to the application code or the Dockerfile in the failing commit's diff. Find what in this Dockerfile makes that plausible, and fix it.
exercises.code:
FROM node:latest
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json .
RUN npm install
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
hints: 'No changes to the Dockerfile in this commit' doesn't mean the Dockerfile resolves to the same thing it did last time it was built -- which instructions here depend on something outside this file and outside this commit?
Two separate things in this file can silently drift over time even with zero edits: the base image tag, and how npm resolves versions with no lockfile involved.

Pin the base image to an exact version, and make sure a lockfile (package-lock.json) is present and actually used (npm ci instead of npm install) so dependency resolution stops being a moving target too.
exercises.solutionCode:
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
exercises.solutionExplanation: FROM node:latest is a floating tag: if CI pulls a fresh base image on a day when latest has moved to a newer Node major version, that can introduce a behavioral or compatibility break with no change in the commit being tested, which matches the 'intermittent, no relevant diff' symptom. npm install resolves version ranges from package.json at install time (and the Dockerfile copies no lockfile), so it can pull a newer transitive dependency on a later date even with an identical package.json. Pinning the base image to an exact tag removes the first source of drift, and npm ci against a committed package-lock.json removes the second: every install reproduces the locked dependency tree, and fails loudly if the lockfile and package.json disagree.

assessments.prompt: Two hosts pull and run the exact same image, referenced by its immutable digest, not just a tag. Which of the following can still legitimately cause the container to behave differently on the two hosts?
options: The versions of OS packages installed via apt-get during the image build.
The host machine's CPU architecture and kernel version.
The environment variables set with fixed values via ENV in the Dockerfile.
The version of the language runtime installed inside the image.
assessments.explanation: CPU architecture and kernel version belong to the host, not the image -- pinning the image by digest guarantees identical file contents, but says nothing about what hardware or kernel is running underneath it, and a mismatch there, such as an arm64 image on an amd64 host or a kernel too old for a feature the app needs, can cause different behavior or an outright failure to run. The “The version of the language runtime installed…”, “The versions of OS packages installed via…”, and “The environment variables set with fixed values…” options are all things the image itself fixes -- the runtime version, the installed package versions, and Dockerfile-set environment variables are all baked into the image's layers and its manifest, so pulling the identical digest gives you the same values for all three on every host.

assessments.prompt: An image built and tested on an Apple Silicon (arm64) laptop is pushed to a registry and pulled onto a standard x86-64 production server, where it immediately fails with "exec format error." What does this demonstrate?
options: The Dockerfile has a syntax error that only manifests on x86-64 hosts.
The image was corrupted in transit during the registry push or pull.
CPU architecture is a property of the host, not the image.
The production server's Docker Engine version is too old to run images built on newer hardware.
assessments.explanation: This is a hardware-level incompatibility, not a bug in the Dockerfile or application code: the image's compiled binaries were built for arm64, and an amd64 kernel cannot execute arm64 machine code. The “The Dockerfile has a syntax error…” option is wrong -- nothing about a Dockerfile's syntax is architecture-dependent; the failure is about compiled binary compatibility, not build instructions. The “The image was corrupted in transit during…” option is wrong -- registry transfers are content-addressed and checksummed; a truncated or corrupted transfer would fail differently, not with this specific, well-known architecture-mismatch error. The “The production server's Docker Engine version…” option is wrong -- Docker Engine version has nothing to do with which CPU instruction sets a given binary was compiled for.

assessments.prompt: A Dockerfile includes `RUN apt-get install -y nginx` with no version pinned. Why can this line undermine build reproducibility even though the Dockerfile's own text never changes between builds?
options: apt-get caches the first version it ever installed and is therefore guaranteed to install that exact version on every subsequent build, forever.
With no version specified, apt-get resolves "nginx" to whatever version the configured package repository currently serves at build time.
This has no real effect on reproducibility, since nginx has no meaningful version differences that could cause a behavioral change.
apt-get always installs the latest major version available anywhere, ignoring the currently configured repository entirely.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer identifies the drift mechanism: an unpinned apt-get install resolves against whatever the package repository currently serves, and that changes as upstream publishes updates, so the same Dockerfile line can produce a different installed version on a later date. The “apt-get always installs the latest major version…” option overstates and misdescribes the mechanism -- it's about resolving against a moving repository state, not some rule about always taking the newest major version specifically. The “apt-get caches the first version it ever…” option is the opposite of what actually happens -- there's no such caching guarantee across separate build invocations. The “This has no real effect on reproducibility…” option is wrong -- nginx, like most real packages, does have version-to-version behavioral differences that can matter, and the whole point of pinning is to not leave that to chance.

assessments.prompt: A colleague says: 'If it works in Docker on my machine, it'll work anywhere.' Explain what part of their environment the container image now controls, and what part it still doesn't, and why that gap matters in practice.
assessments.modelAnswer: The image controls everything that lives inside its own layers: the exact language runtime version, the exact versions of any OS packages and application dependencies that were installed during the build, every file the application ships with, and any environment variables or configuration baked in via the Dockerfile. Pull that same image -- ideally referenced by digest, or at minimum by a version tag that was itself built from pinned dependencies -- on any other host, and all of that is identical, which is the class of bug ('different OpenSSL,' 'different Python patch version,' 'a system package I forgot I had installed') that containers eliminate well. What the image does not control is anything that belongs to the host running it: the host's kernel version and the syscalls/features it supports, the host's CPU architecture (an arm64-built image simply will not run on an amd64 host, and vice versa), and the host's available resources like memory and CPU, which can cause a workload to behave very differently or get OOM-killed on a smaller host even from an identical image. In practice this gap matters at two edges people forget: deploying an image built on a developer's Apple Silicon laptop to x86-64 production infrastructure, which is an architecture mismatch and not a bug in the app, and running a container built on a modern base image on a production host with an unusually old kernel that's missing a feature the container's software assumes. So the accurate version of the claim is: it eliminates almost every environment-drift bug in the userspace we packaged, but the host's kernel, architecture, and resources are still variables outside the container's control.
